item.title: Genomic work helps find treatment for rare blood disorder
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, genomic breakthrough

Genomic work helps find treatment for rare blood disorder

Sisters with a rare blood condition are the first patients to receive a repurposed drug to treat it, after a team of doctors and cardiovascular scientists used genomic sequencing to identify the drug's target.

The research, which includes findings from the successful treatment in two adult sisters living in the West Midlands in the U.K., is published in the Blood Journal. The work was led by professor Neil Morgan from the University of Birmingham, Dr. Manoj Raghavan from University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust and Dr. Hrushikesh Vyas, who carried out laboratory tests as part of his Ph.D. at the University of Birmingham.

The condition is called SRC-related thrombocytopenia, which is a very rare disorder that causes a gene to constantly express a protein involved in platelet production and activation. Patients have abnormally low levels of platelets and often develop an enlarged spleen, immune issues and scarring in their bone marrow where blood cells are made. Existing treatment options have largely focused on supplementing low platelets through blood transfusions, which require regular hospital trips.

Following work to understand the mechanism involved in SRC-related thrombocytopenia using genetic testing, the team was able to identify that dasatinib, used in blood cancer treatment, could dampen down the SRC protein's activity and help patients have more typical platelet production by reversing the bone marrow damage.

Morgan, from the University of Birmingham and lead author of the study, said, "Advances in genomics have meant we have been able to identify how an existing drug used in cancer therapy can treat this specific rare blood condition. The findings themselves have already made a difference for these patients, but also show the way forward using genomics to identify how medicines already in use can make a difference for the many rare diseases and conditions that currently aren't treatable.

"The work which has changed the sisters' day-to-day lives is thanks to the close working between the university and hospital through Birmingham Health Partners and Cancer Research UK."

Raghavan, a consultant hematologist from University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust who treated the two sisters, said, "This is a lovely example of how translational research can transform patients' lives. Genomics identified a mutation that we were able to target by repurposing a drug usually used to treat a type of leukemia. Even though this is a rare condition, it gives an insight into how the bone marrow works that can be taken forward for other blood diseases."

It's great now—although I never stopped traveling. Manjit's story

Since starting the treatment around three years ago, dasatinib has helped Manjit Kaur improve her blood counts and stop needing transfusions. Now, Kaur has felt less tired and has been able to continue her two passions—traveling and working in her local health center.

Kaur began taking dasatinib after her sister, who has the same condition, responded well to the treatment. After starting on the drug and working out the right amount for her alongside her Crohn's disease, Kaur now takes a dose she can manage and has regular blood tests at hospital every three months. Her blood counts have improved, and she no longer needs transfusions.

"I mean, I've never let it stop me doing anything," Kaur says. "I've always carried on working and traveling. But it's great to not have to go in (to hospital) for regular transfusions."

Kaur, who lives in the West Midlands, was diagnosed with SRC in 1989, in her late teens or early 20s. She believes she may have had the condition for several years before it was identified. At the time, she often felt tired and bruised easily, but thought the symptoms were part of living with Crohn's disease, which she had been diagnosed with as a child.

Her childhood was shaped by hospital visits and time away from school. She was treated in Wolverhampton, at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London and later in Birmingham. Kaur missed many lessons and left school without sitting her final exams.

She later completed training courses, gained qualifications and built a career in administration. For the past 31 years, she has worked as an IT administrator at a general practitioner's office, where she also completed a foundation degree in information and communication technologies.

Kaur hopes her experience will encourage others to consider taking part in clinical trials or trying a treatment offered to them. "Give it a go," she says. "If it doesn't work, you can stop. And you're helping other people, because doctors can learn what works for others too."

Publication details

Hrushikesh Vyas et al., Dasatinib is a novel therapy for SRC-related thrombocytopenia, Blood Journal (2026). DOI: 10.1182/blood.2026035087

Journal information: Blood

item.title: When is it time to treat obesity? An expert explains it's not just a lack of willpower
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: expert explanation, useful context

When is it time to treat obesity? An expert explains it's not just a lack of willpower

If you're trying to figure out how to treat obesity, the choices can feel overwhelming. Diet plans, weight-loss surgery, newer pills and weekly injections all promise results, and it's hard to know when and where to start.

HealthDay sat down for an exclusive interview with Dr. Rachel Batterham, senior vice president of cardiometabolic health at Eli Lilly and Co., at the health care innovation conference HLTH USA 2026 in Las Vegas.

She talked about why lost weight is so hard to keep off and how to choose a treatment that fits your life.

Her first message: Obesity isn't a failure of willpower.

"For many years people just viewed obesity as a lifestyle choice," Batterham said. "I can promise you nobody would choose to have severe obesity."

For most of human history, food was scarce, she explained, so the body is wired to eat whenever food is around. Today, people are surrounded by food cues. And when you diet, your body treats it like a famine.

"They can lose the weight," Batterham said. "But then the biology kicks in to fight against it."

So what should you consider when thinking about obesity treatments?

Batterham suggests starting with lifestyle basics, such as cutting back on ultraprocessed foods and looking at physical activity, stress and sleep.

The next question is whether extra weight is affecting your health.

Where you carry it matters, she said. Weight around the belly is more closely tied to high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and heart disease than weight in other places. A family history of those conditions or of severe obesity also raises the stakes.

"It really comes down to what's the health outcome, not necessarily the numbers on the scale," she said.

For years, Batterham led a bariatric surgery center in the U.K. to treat people struggling with obesity.

"One of the things about bariatric surgery is that from the moment you have the surgery, then your appetite is completely reduced," she said.

She explained that after surgery, hormones like GLP-1s go up and this helps drive the marked weight loss after the procedure.

This hormone connection is how newer obesity medications entered the treatment landscape.

Anyone considering medication should know it's likely to be a lifelong treatment, Batterham added. Stopping usually means regaining the weight, much like blood pressure climbs again when someone quits blood pressure pills.

There's no one-size-fits-all option, she said. Someone who travels often, for example, may prefer a pill over carrying an injection pen.

Batterham walks patients through the choices and expected benefits, then often asks them to talk it over with loved ones, since the whole household is involved.

Most of today's drugs are GLP-1 medicines, which mimic a gut hormone that curbs appetite.

They aren't right for everyone. Stomach and gut side effects are the most common, so people who already have digestive problems should be cautious. The drugs can't be used during pregnancy, so women hoping to conceive need careful planning.

Raising the dose too fast can cause nausea, diarrhea or constipation, so slower is often better, Batterham said. Patients also need enough protein and fluids.

However, with the right support and instructions, she said, "patients tend to do very well."

item.title: Nature walks 'another tool' in mental health fight
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, mental health intervention

Nature walks 'another tool' in mental health fight

People struggling with their mental health are being encouraged to connect with nature on their doorstep.

Hope Haven, in Whitehaven, west Cumbria, opened in March as one of six pilot centres across the country dedicated to tackling problems before they escalate.

It has now joined forces with the RSPB to issue "nature prescriptions", which see people encouraged to visit a number of places in the area, such as the local harbour, sand dunes at Ravenglass and Walkmill Community Woodland at Moresby.

Clinical manager Barbara Slater said the scheme was "another tool" to add to the hub's range of interventions.

Visitors to Hope Haven, located in a former bank building in the town centre, are able to discuss their concerns with mental health professionals without needing a referral.

Slater said the nature prescriptions, a series of suggestions for local walks and activities contained in a booklet, were "a great way to gently introduce nature and well-being into people's lives".

"Being close to the Lake District, people often think that to go out in nature you need special equipment and boots," she said.

"We purposefully tailored it to Copeland, putting suggestions in for places that can be reached by public transport and most are free.

"That was really important because we want people to feel they're not excluded."

Other featured locations include Whitehaven's Castle Park, Seascale seafront and St Bees Head, home to a breeding site for guillemots.

'Moment of joy'

Not all suggestions contained in the booklet required travel, however.

"It can be as simple as being outside and breathing the air," Slater said.

"Another is to look at raindrops on a window and watch the water roll down. It's about connecting with something much bigger than ourselves."

Hope Haven is the first organisation in Cumbria to take part in the scheme.

Staff training and the production of the booklets has been funded with Â£5,500 secured via partner organisations including the NHS, National Lottery and West Cumbria Rivers Trust.

Sarah Walker, nature and well-being manager at RSPB England, said the charity's trials had shown "even taking a moment or two to notice nature can boost mental and physical health".

"So many people face a whole range of pressures in their lives and nature could provide a way to help them through and find a moment of joy in their day," she added.

More than 5,000 people have visited Hope Haven since its opening with that number prompting conflicting emotions, Slater said.

"We're very busy because the community is coming to see us, but there's also a sadness because it shows there are struggles with a range of issues - anxiety, feeling in crisis, debt and alcohol problems.

"We try to help people in those really dark places."

item.title: 'We feed and wash her': Severe ME leaves woman bedbound for five years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, personal story, rare condition

'We feed and wash her': Severe ME leaves woman bedbound for five years

Rowena Davies had been planning to travel the world with her partner until an ME diagnosis left her unable to talk or leave her bed.

The 42-year-old, known as Row, initially thought she was burnt out, but after years of searching for answers was finally diagnosed in 2021 and her partner Shauna Chambers has since given up work to help the family care for her.

Campaigners are warning that people with severe ME - sometimes referred to clinically as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome - could die without changes to services in Wales.

The Welsh government said proposals for an allâWales specialist, an expert group and national standards were being considered.

It is estimated more than 400,000 people across the UK have ME, a complex multi-system condition with no known cure.

Shauna, 34, said: "She had a cough that didn't leave for many months, but the main thing was that she would be absolutely drained and exhausted after doing such small things.

"Now, she really isn't able to do anything at all."

Shauna, from Tywyn in Gwynedd, said Row was "full of energy" and loved sport, but now she cannot tolerate light or noise, and any exertion will cause her to deteriorate.

"We feed her, we wash her, we brush her teeth. We were left to navigate this on our own," she said.

"It's like you're grieving someone that is still alive, and you sit next to her sometimes, and all you can do is just hold her hand and breathe.

"People's lives have been completely ruined by this condition, and if nothing changes people can die from ME, and it is absolutely avoidable."

Campaigners told BBC Wales in March that healthcare services were "like a desert" for those most severely affected.

With the right support, Row's family are hopeful she can get better. She recently had her first visit by the Living Well service within Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which has been expanded to include ME, and now aims to support people living with any severity of the condition.

It uses funding from the Welsh government's Adferiad programme, external but campaigners say that services vary between health boards. There is no clinical lead for ME in Wales.

John Peters, 65, from Swansea, was diagnosed with the condition 40 years ago. He was once a keen rugby player, but after a virus, his life changed.

"I've gone through improvements, and then got another infection, and that's been the cycle of my life since 1985," he said.

"One of the hardest things is the loss of identity. You're not a husband, a father, you don't have a career.

"Your life goes past and then you realise what's happened. I hate the illness.

"No one knows what I've been through. There is no care for me."

Swansea Bay University Health Board said its service, also funded by the Adferiad programme, "focuses on improving quality of life, supporting independence, and enabling individuals to manage the impact of ME within their own daily circumstances" while "recognising the fluctuating nature of the condition and the importance of personalised care".

What is myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME)?

ME is a chronic and complex multi-system condition, which causes symptoms such as extreme fatigue and post-exertional malaise.

That means simple physical or mental activities can leave people completely debilitated.

Not everyone with ME is affected in the same way. There is a spectrum of severity, which is often categorised as mild, moderate, severe and very severe.

While researchers are still investigating the causes, triggers may include infection or other illness. There is no specific treatment.

Source: NHS

'People do die from severe ME'

Liverpool-based private consultant Dr Binita Kane, who has a special interest in ME and long Covid, said she had a growing waiting list of patients across the UK.

"I think that is a sad reflection on the fact that the services, sadly, don't exist at the moment in the way they need to through the NHS," she said.

"Even if patients can access a service, they often can't access medications and treatments for symptom control and support for overlapping conditions because there aren't doctors integrated into those services."

She said the goal is always "to prevent people from getting into the very severe state" through early intervention, but she said that certain investigations can happen at people's homes, such as 24-hour ECG tests, sleep studies and blood tests.

"People sadly do die from severe ME for different reasons, it is a risk, and ME is one of the only conditions I'm aware of where the more sick you are, the less access to treatment and help and support you get," she added.

"These are young people whose lives have been decimated, destroyed, who aren't getting enough help, care, and support.

"There's a million reasons why the government should be taking this extremely seriously."

Campaign groups in Wales have joined together to call on the government to bring together a national expert group, appoint an all-Wales clinical lead, and develop a research strategy.

In a recent survey of more than 5,400 people across the UK, 62.1% of respondents in Wales reported having no NHS specialist ME service in their area, compared with 32.8% in England.

Action for ME, who conducted the survey, said the findings demonstrate that "access to specialist care remains a postcode lottery".

"People have been waiting for decades and that is too long" said the charity's chief executive Sonya Chowdhury.

She said that a cross-party debate was held in the Senedd in December 2025 in which the current health minister, Plaid Cymru's Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, advocated on behalf of ME patients while in opposition.

"We are 12 months on, and we are yet to see action," she added.

"It's fantastic that the minister has met with us and other groups here in Wales, and we have heard some positive noises, but what we need to see now is something changing."…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, leadership change, health board

Health board chief executive drops new NHS job after critical report

The chief executive of Wales's largest health board will no longer take up a new post in England, following a damning review of her current organisation's leadership.

Carol Shillabeer, who has been Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board's chief executive since May 2023, had been due to lead the Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Trust in England in the new year.

But a review into the Welsh health board found that, in some parts, targets and money had a "greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

The Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said the "seriousness of the findings" could not be ignored and Shillabeer made the "personal decision" to withdraw from the role.

Dyfed Edwards, chair of Betsi Cadwaladr health board, confirmed Shillabeer would leave her current post on 3 January 2027. He thanked her for her service and wished her well for the future.

Confirming Shillabeer's withdrawal from the role, the Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said it had "taken our time to carefully consider the situation and discuss the matter" with her.

"Carol feels that this is the best course of action for the sake of the patients, our communities, and LSCFT staff."

"We agree with her decision and wish her the best for the future," it added.

A spokesperson said that a board of trustees would consider the next steps regarding the appointment of a new chief executive.

Shillabeer spent three and a half years leading the health board, which covers all of north Wales. She was appointed after the Welsh government put it into "special measures" for the second time in its history.

It has been under the highest level of oversight due to concerns about care quality, patient safety and leadership.

The independent review published on Tuesday found the health board lacked "the organisational conditions necessary to reliably deliver and sustain improvement".

It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

It also said the health board had a "dedicated and loyal" workforce, with a "high level of expertise" across many services, as well as the capacity to provide strong local services.

The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".

Responding to the document, Health Minister, Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, rejected calls for "radical action or structural change".

Instead, he suggested that "stability" is needed following a period characterised by "too much change."

item.title: Reform UK pledges to scrap hospital parking fees in England
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, policy change, hospital parking

Reform UK pledges to scrap hospital parking fees in England

Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.

The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to Â£20 a day for parking spots.

It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the Â£300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.

The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.

Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.

Echoing a line traditionally used by British politicians to claim stewardship of the health service, he said: "What we are saying is that the NHS is safe in our hands".

Parking rules

Parking at hospitals in Wales and Scotland is largely free, but NHS trusts in England are allowed to charge and set their own fees and rules.

Government guidance means parking is free for disabled people holding Blue Badges, frequent outpatients, parents of sick children staying overnight and NHS staff working night shifts.

But most visitors are generally expected to pay, along with staff working day shifts.

Reform says its policy to compensate NHS trusts would cost Â£285m a year to deliver, assuming a Â£25m annual saving from payment collection costs that would not longer be required.

It plans to recoup lost revenue by charging overseas visitors 200% of the national tariff for NHS services, instead of 150% currently, and extending charges to A&E visits, ambulance services and GP care.

It also says it would make all foreign visitors from countries that do not have reciprocal healthcare arrangements with the UK take out travel insurance covering NHS care, allowing it to "more aggressively collect" money due.

Private contractors

Siva Anandaciva, policy director at the King's Fund health think tank, said parking fees could be a "burden" for those visiting hospitals, but questioned whether Reform's proposals would raise enough to fully compensate trusts.

He said the additional charges on visitors for care would bring extra administration costs, whilst hospitals would need to spend money on systems to ensure free spaces were available to those who need them most.

The experience in Scotland had shown it can also take an "awfully long time" for hospitals to exit contracts with private firms running car pars, he said.

He added: "You might not end up saving as much money as you think".

The health department said it expected fees charged by trusts to be "reasonable and in line with the local area".

"Where charges do apply, the money made is used to maintain facilities, with surplus income put back into the NHS to benefit both staff and patients," a spokesperson added.

In response to parliamentary questions earlier this year, the department also argued, external fees were a "significant control mechanism" to manage capacity given the limited number of car parking spaces available.

item.title: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, young hikers, mental health

The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline

After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.

He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.

"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."

Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.

Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.

Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.

Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.

"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.

"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.

'Grounding'

Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".

"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.

After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.

"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."

She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.

Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".

Friendship flux

Walking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield.

"They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.

As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."

Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.

For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week.

"I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."

For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down.

"There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.

Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.

To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee.

In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old.

"There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."

Not everyone can access green space easily or has the time to go hiking because of work or childcare commitments.

Here are Longman's tips for getting your nature fix as close as possible to home:

- Move in nature - an urban park or garden will do

- Listen to the sounds of the elements, like wind, rain, birdsong

- Smell the distinctive scent of pine forests, breathe in the outdoors

- If you are indoors, bring the sounds and imagery of nature into your home using apps

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, flu surge, public health

NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge

A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles â whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.
